A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. If the manifest switched first, a browser could fetch it and request files that aren't there yet, which means broken pages. Uploading first means every name the new manifest mentions already exists when the switch happens. The switch then becomes the single moment the release goes live.

The old assets stay because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it names. Since every release uses new versioned names, the old files aren't overwritten, so those browsers keep getting a consistent set of files. Delete the old files and those browsers break until they pick up the new manifest.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. Once it changes, any browser that loads it immediately requests the new names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get 404s and a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when the manifest goes live, so the switch is effectively atomic.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Those pages still request the old names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or fetching an image later in the session. Deleting the old files would break those users mid-session. Since every release uses new versioned names, old and new files never collide, so both can be served at the same time.

Every release uploads its new assets under versioned names, so they never overwrite the files the live site is using. Only after the upload is complete do we switch the manifest to point at those new names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the upload finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that aren't there yet, which breaks the page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when it goes live.

We keep the old assets because some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep requesting the files it names. Deleting those files would break pages for those users mid-session. Leaving them in place lets those browsers finish with the old version while new visitors get the new one.

A release has two steps. First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so nothing already live gets overwritten. Then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the uploads finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that don't exist yet. That means broken pages, missing styles or scripts, and no way to fix it from the browser's side. With the upload first, every name the new manifest mentions already exists when the switch happens. The switch becomes the single moment the release goes live, and anyone who loads it gets a complete set of files.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep asking for the files it lists. If we deleted those files, those users would get failed requests in the middle of a session, even though they did nothing wrong. Because the new assets use different names, the old ones never get in the way. Both versions can be served at the same time, and each browser gets a consistent set that matches the manifest it has.
